title: Grade 11 Physics — Laws of Motion
description: Chapter 5: Newton's laws, friction, momentum, impulse, equilibrium
subject: physics

questions.question: Newton's First Law of Motion is also called the:
questions.explanation: Newton's First Law (Law of Inertia): a body at rest stays at rest, and a body in uniform motion continues in uniform motion, unless acted upon by an external net force.

questions.question: Newton's Second Law of Motion states F = :
questions.explanation: F = ma (net force = mass × acceleration). More precisely: F = dp/dt (rate of change of momentum), which reduces to F = ma for constant mass.

questions.question: A body of mass 5 kg is acted upon by a net force of 20 N. What is the acceleration?
questions.explanation: a = F/m = 20/5 = 4 m/s². This is a direct application of Newton's Second Law.

questions.question: Newton's Third Law states:
options: An object at rest stays at rest unless acted upon by force
For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
The total momentum of a closed system is conserved
questions.explanation: Newton's Third Law: forces always come in equal-and-opposite pairs acting on DIFFERENT objects. When you push a wall, the wall pushes you back with equal force.

questions.question: What is linear momentum?
options: Product of mass and velocity (p = mv)
questions.explanation: Linear momentum p = mv. It is a vector quantity. The SI unit is kg·m/s. Newton's Second Law can be written as F = Δp/Δt.

questions.question: The law of conservation of momentum states:
options: In the absence of external forces, the total momentum of a system remains constant
Momentum is always zero in a closed system
questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum: if ΣF_ext = 0, then Δp_total = 0. This is why a gun recoils when fired — the system's total momentum before and after must be equal.

questions.question: The coefficient of friction (μ) is defined as:
options: The ratio of mass to normal force
The ratio of friction force to normal reaction force (f/N)
The ratio of velocity to acceleration
The ratio of applied force to area
questions.explanation: μ = f/N. The coefficient of kinetic friction (μk) is slightly less than the coefficient of static friction (μs). It depends on the nature of the surfaces, not on the area of contact.

questions.question: Two objects collide and stick together (perfectly inelastic). Object A: 2 kg at 6 m/s; Object B: 4 kg at rest. What is the final velocity?
questions.explanation: Conservation of momentum: m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ = (m₁+m₂)v. (2)(6) + (4)(0) = 6v. v = 12/6 = 2 m/s.

questions.question: Static friction is greater than kinetic friction because:
options: Static surfaces are always rougher than moving ones
Molecular bonds and interlocking surface asperities form when surfaces are at rest, requiring more force to break them than to keep them sliding
Kinetic friction depends on velocity, which is zero when static
The normal force is greater when a body is stationary
questions.explanation: When surfaces are at rest, molecular adhesion and mechanical interlocking increase the friction. Once sliding begins, fewer contact bonds form at any instant, reducing the friction force.

questions.question: A 10 kg object is on a surface with μs = 0.3. What is the maximum static friction force? (g = 10 m/s²)
questions.explanation: Maximum static friction = μs × N = μs × mg = 0.3 × 10 × 10 = 30 N. The applied force must exceed 30 N to start the object moving.

questions.question: What is an impulse?
options: A large force acting over a long period
The change in momentum: Impulse = F × Δt = Δp
The average speed during a collision
Kinetic energy transferred during a collision
questions.explanation: Impulse = FΔt = Δ(mv). This is why car airbags work — they increase the collision time, reducing the peak force on the occupant (same impulse = same momentum change, but spread over longer time).

questions.question: In which type of collision is kinetic energy conserved?
questions.explanation: In elastic collisions, both momentum AND kinetic energy are conserved. Billiard ball collisions approximate elastic collisions. In all other collisions, some KE is converted to heat, sound, or deformation.

questions.question: A gun recoils when fired. Which law explains this?
questions.explanation: The gun exerts a forward force on the bullet (action); the bullet exerts an equal backward force on the gun (reaction), causing recoil. Total momentum before = 0 = total momentum after.

questions.question: For a particle to be in equilibrium, the condition is:
options: Vector sum of all forces acting on it = 0 (ΣF = 0)
Both net velocity and acceleration must be 0 simultaneously
questions.explanation: Equilibrium means ΣF = 0 (and Στ = 0 for rotational equilibrium). A body can be in equilibrium while moving at constant velocity (dynamic equilibrium) — it doesn't have to be stationary.

questions.question: A rocket accelerates by expelling gas at 500 m/s at a rate of 10 kg/s. What is the thrust force?
questions.explanation: Thrust = (dm/dt) × v_exhaust = 10 × 500 = 5000 N. This is a direct application of Newton's Third Law and the rocket equation.

questions.question: The angle of friction is the angle whose tangent equals:
options: The ratio of normal force to weight
The coefficient of friction (tan θ = μ)
The angle of the inclined plane
The ratio of kinetic to static friction
questions.explanation: Angle of friction θ = tan⁻¹(μ). It is the angle between the normal reaction and the resultant of normal reaction and friction. It equals the angle of repose — the maximum angle before an object slides.

questions.question: A pseudo force in a non-inertial (accelerating) reference frame is:
options: A real contact force caused by friction
A fictitious force introduced so Newton's laws can be applied in an accelerating reference frame
Equal in magnitude and direction to the reaction force
The gravitational force acting on objects in the frame
questions.explanation: When you're in an accelerating car and feel 'pushed back', that's a pseudo force (= -ma). It's not a real force — it's an artefact of the non-inertial frame. Real forces always have a physical source.

questions.question: A block rests on a 30° incline. μs = 0.4, g = 10 m/s². Does the block slide? (sin30° = 0.5, cos30° = 0.866)
options: No — static friction always prevents sliding on inclines
Yes — gravity component along incline (mgsin30°) exceeds maximum static friction (μmgcos30°)
No — the block is too heavy to slide
Yes — kinetic friction is less than gravity, so the block must slide
questions.explanation: For a 10 kg block: mgsin30° = 100×0.5 = 50 N; max static friction = μmgcos30° = 0.4×100×0.866 = 34.6 N. Since 50 N > 34.6 N, the block slides.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes the condition for a ball thrown horizontally to hit the ground?
options: The horizontal velocity determines the fall time
The height alone determines the fall time (vertical free fall: t = √(2h/g))
Both horizontal velocity and height equally determine fall time
The mass of the ball determines how quickly it falls
questions.explanation: Horizontal and vertical motions are independent. The ball falls under gravity regardless of horizontal velocity. t = √(2h/g) — only height matters for fall time.

questions.question: What is the 'normal force' when a 5 kg book rests on a table? (g = 10 m/s²)
options: 50 N upward (equal and opposite to the book's weight)
questions.explanation: Normal force = weight = mg = 5×10 = 50 N. By Newton's Third Law, the table pushes up on the book with exactly 50 N — equal and opposite to the book's weight — keeping it in equilibrium.
